title: The lute string
hookLine: Sona strains too hard; the Buddha asks how a lute sounds when its strings are too tight or too loose (AN 6.55)

cards: On the walking path in a forest called the Cool Grove, a young monk has been pacing back and forth for so long that his feet are bleeding. The path behind him is stained. His name is Sona.
He grew up wealthy and sheltered, and he's decided to make up for it by trying harder than anyone else. And right in the middle of all that effort, he's thinking about quitting.
On day twenty you met the image at the heart of this story. Today, the whole story.

teach.b: Sona's thought, the sutta says, runs like this: I'm one of the most energetic of the Buddha's disciples, and still my mind isn't free. My family has wealth. I could go home, enjoy it, and do good with it.
The Buddha knows what he's thinking and comes to him. He doesn't scold or push. He asks about music.
Sona, before you went forth, weren't you skilled at the lute? Yes, sir. When its strings were too tight, did it sound right?
No, sir. Too loose? No, sir.

And tuned to an even pitch, neither too tight nor too loose? Then it sounded right, sir. Just so, the Buddha says: effort that's too strong leads to restlessness, and effort that's too slack leads to laziness.

Settle on an even pitch of effort, and tune the rest of your practice to it. The vīṇā, the Indian lute, isn't a random choice. Sona knows it with his hands; the Buddha teaches him in the language of his own skill.
And it matters for the four efforts. Effort isn't a dial that only turns up. Some days the string is slack, and you need to rouse yourself.

teach.h: EASE OFF, OR TURN IT UP.
teach.b: Some days it's wound so tight it buzzes, and you need to ease off.
The sutta says Sona took this to heart, practiced with balance, and before long became an arahant, fully awakened. The walking path stayed the same. The tuning changed.

how: Meditation teachers across Buddhist traditions tell Sona's story to students who push too hard or drift, and encourage them to adjust effort through a sit rather than force it.

games.why: in AN 6.55 the Buddha asks whether a lute plays well too tight or too loose, and tells Sona to settle on an even pitch of effort.

practice: Check the string: if the body is tight, jaw set, shoulders up, ease it a quarter turn and let the breath happen; if it's slack and drifting, sit up a little and feel the breath more clearly.
Keep tuning gently through the sit, a little looser, a little tighter, listening for the even note.

wordCard.voice: Vina, the Indian lute. The Buddha's lesson for Sona: effort too tight brings restlessness, too loose brings laziness. Tune it to an even pitch.

orig.note: Pali and Sanskrit vīṇā: the Indian lute, whose strings the Buddha uses to teach balanced effort.
